title: Beautiful Arrangement
summary: Given an integer n, determine the count of permutations of integers from 1 to n where each element perm[i] either divides i or i divides perm[i].
statement: Given an integer n, determine the count of permutations of integers from 1 to n where each element perm[i] either divides i or i divides perm[i].
constraints: 1 <= n <= 15. Use every integer from 1 through n exactly once.
Positions are 1-indexed. At every position i, value % i == 0 OR i % value == 0 must hold.
Return the number of valid permutations, not the permutations themselves.
hints: Place one unused number at the next position, then recursively complete the remaining positions.
The set of used values determines the next position. Cache the number of completions for that set.
visit(mask): if every value is used return 1; otherwise sum visit(mask|bit) for each unused value satisfying either divisibility rule at popcount(mask)+1.
Use 1-based positions for divisibility even if the allowed-mask array is 0-based. Each choice consumes one distinct value; a completed permutation contributes exactly one.
editorial: Recursive search partitions valid permutations by their next value, without overlap because every value is used once. The next position follows from the number of set bits, so the used-value mask completely identifies a subproblem. Memoization gives O(n*2^n) time and O(2^n) storage, including a recursion depth of at most 15. All 15 legal n values are tested: two visible and thirteen hidden. An independent inclusion-exclusion permanent counts bijective allowed position/value assignments, and literal permutation enumeration checks small n.

tests.explanation: Both [1,2] and [2,1] work. In the second arrangement, position 2 is divisible by its value 1; either direction of divisibility suffices.
Only [1] exists, and 1 divides 1. Count this arrangement once, even though both divisibility checks hold.
